abstract: Brookings Metro and Opportunity@Work analyze how AI may reshape career pathways for America's approximately 70 million STARs (workers Skilled Through Alternative Routes, without four-year degrees). Using Anthropic's observed-exposure measure mapped onto Opportunity@Work's pathway taxonomy, the study finds that 15.6 million STARs work in roles in the top quartile of AI exposure, representing 43% of all top-quartile workers nationally. Nearly 11 million of these are in Gateway occupations — the stepping-stone roles connecting entry-level to higher-wage Destination jobs — with just six Gateway occupations accounting for approximately 8 million workers. STARs are 62.3% of all Gateway-occupation workers. Across Destination occupations, 12.9 million workers (roughly one-third) are highly exposed, including sales representatives, accountants, and financial managers. Only 51% of Gateway-to-Destination career pathways avoid high AI exposure, meaning nearly half of traditional advancement routes face disruption. The study identifies 3.5 million STARs who are both highly exposed AND have low adaptive capacity (67% of all such doubly vulnerable workers), while 23 million STARs overall have low adaptive capacity (68% of the national total). Geographic analysis reveals highest pathway exposure in Sun Belt metros: Palm Bay FL (35.5%), Cape Coral FL (34.7%), Jacksonville (33%), and Northeast state capitals like Albany NY (32.8%). Since 73% of US workers live and work in the same county, disruption and remediation will be place-specific.
keyFindings: 15.6 million STARs work in top-quartile AI-exposed roles, constituting 43% of all workers in the most exposed occupations nationally.
Only 51% of Gateway-to-Destination career pathways avoid high AI exposure, meaning nearly half of traditional advancement routes for non-degree workers face disruption.
3.5 million STARs are both highly AI-exposed and have low adaptive capacity, representing 67% of all doubly vulnerable workers.
STARs are 62.3% of Gateway occupation workers, making non-degree workers disproportionately concentrated in the stepping-stone roles most at risk from AI.

Highest pathway-exposure metros are in the Sun Belt: Palm Bay FL (35.5%), Cape Coral FL (34.7%), Jacksonville (33%), with disruption inherently place-specific since 73% of workers live and work in the same county.
methodology: The study applies Anthropic's observed-exposure measure (estimating task-level AI capability from real Claude usage data) to Opportunity@Work's career pathway taxonomy, which maps Gateway occupations (stepping stones) to Destination occupations (higher-wage goals). Analysis uses O*NET task data, BLS occupational employment statistics, and American Community Survey geographic data. Adaptive capacity assessed through skills transferability and local labor market conditions. Metropolitan-level exposure calculated across 100+ metro areas.
qualifiers: AI exposure measures capability and current usage, not inevitable displacement — actual outcomes depend on employer decisions, policy responses, and demand elasticity. The Opportunity@Work pathway taxonomy represents historical career transitions and may not reflect future labor market structures. Adaptive capacity measurement is inherently uncertain and depends on local factors. The observed-exposure measure from Anthropic reflects Claude usage specifically, which may not represent all AI tool adoption. The analysis focuses on STARs by design, meaning the 43% and 67% figures describe shares within specific population subgroups rather than the general workforce.
